cursor.description: Opaque pagination cursor from a previous response (nextCursor). Omit to start from the beginning.

title: List templates

To find a template, follow `pagination.nextCursor` until `hasNextPage` is false: a name missing from one page may be on a later one.

limit.description: Maximum number of items to return (default 20, max 100). Use the returned nextCursor to fetch the next page.

cursor.description: Opaque pagination cursor from a previous response (nextCursor). Omit to start from the beginning.

name: run-endpoint
title: Submit Serverless job
description: Submit an asynchronous job to a Serverless endpoint. Returns a job ID immediately — use get-job-status to poll for results (pass its `wait` to block through a cold start instead of tight-looping). Async results are available for 30 minutes after completion.

endpointId.description: ID of the Serverless endpoint to run

input.description: Input payload for the worker handler. The expected fields depend on the deployed model or worker.

webhook.description: Webhook URL to receive job completion notifications instead of polling

ttl.description: Time-to-live for the job result in milliseconds

s3Config.description: S3-compatible storage config for large outputs

name: runsync-endpoint
title: Run Serverless job and wait
description: Submit a synchronous job to a Serverless endpoint and wait for the result. Best for fast tasks: if the job outlives the wait, the response returns a job ID and a non-terminal status (IN_QUEUE or IN_PROGRESS) to poll with get-job-status. Max payload 20 MB; results expire after 1 minute. The wait parameter extends the server-side wait — this server runs behind a 60-second gateway deadline, so waits clamp to 45000 ms, which is also the effective default. For longer jobs use run-endpoint + get-job-status.

endpointId.description: ID of the Serverless endpoint to run synchronously

input.description: Input payload for the worker handler. The expected fields depend on the deployed model or worker.

wait.description: How long in milliseconds the server should wait for a result (1000–45000; higher values clamp to 45000, the gateway ceiling).

webhook.description: Webhook URL to receive job completion notifications instead of polling

ttl.description: Time-to-live for the job result in milliseconds

s3Config.description: S3-compatible storage config for large outputs

name: get-job-status
title: Get job status
description: Check the status of a Serverless job. Returns the current status and output when complete. Job statuses: IN_QUEUE, IN_PROGRESS, COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELLED, TIMED_OUT. Pass `wait` (milliseconds, up to 45000) to BLOCK server-side, polling until the job reaches a terminal status or the budget expires — use it to ride out a cold start (a first job on a fresh worker pulls the image and loads the model, commonly 1–5+ minutes) in a single call instead of returning on the first IN_QUEUE and tight-looping the tool. Without `wait` it returns the current status immediately (a single check). If the budget expires before a terminal status, it returns the latest non-terminal status with pollingTimedOut:true — call again (with `wait`) to keep blocking. IMPORTANT: a job stuck IN_QUEUE does not necessarily mean a capacity shortage — a worker may have spun up and crash-looped. When the job is IN_QUEUE this tool attaches a workerHealth summary and a hint. To dig deeper call list-endpoint-workers, then read stream-worker-logs regardless of the status a worker reports: a container failing to start loops while its worker still shows RUNNING or THROTTLED and unhealthy stays 0, so UNHEALTHY is one symptom of a crash loop and not a test for it. The logs are the authority.

endpointId.description: ID of the Serverless endpoint the job belongs to

jobId.description: ID of the job to check

wait.description: How long in milliseconds to block server-side, polling the job until it reaches a terminal status (1000–45000). Omit for a single immediate check. Use this to wait through a cold start rather than tight-looping the tool.

name: stream-job
title: Stream job output
description: Retrieve streaming output from a Serverless job. The worker must support streaming output. Polls /stream/{jobId} and collects chunks until the status is COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELLED, or TIMED_OUT, for up to 45 seconds. If the budget expires first, returns the chunks collected so far with pollingTimedOut: true — call stream-job again to resume where it left off, or get-job-status to check without streaming.

endpointId.description: ID of the Serverless endpoint the job belongs to

jobId.description: ID of the job to stream results from

name: cancel-job
title: Cancel job
description: Cancel a Serverless job that is queued or in progress.

endpointId.description: ID of the Serverless endpoint the job belongs to

jobId.description: ID of the job to cancel

name: retry-job
title: Retry job
description: Retry a failed or timed-out Serverless job. Only works for jobs with FAILED or TIMED_OUT status. The previous output is removed and the job is requeued.

endpointId.description: ID of the Serverless endpoint the job belongs to

jobId.description: ID of the job to retry

name: endpoint-health
title: Get endpoint health
description: Get the endpoint-level health rollup for a Serverless endpoint: worker counts by state plus job queue statistics. This is the runtime plane's own /health view and it can lag or disagree with the per-worker truth — when a job is stuck IN_QUEUE, prefer list-endpoint-workers over this rollup for per-worker state — but treat neither as the authority on crash loops, because a container failing to start loops while its worker reports RUNNING or THROTTLED and unhealthy stays 0; stream-worker-logs is what settles it, and note that get-job-status already attaches that worker summary and a hint on every IN_QUEUE result. Zero workers here means the endpoint is waiting for GPU capacity.

endpointId.description: ID of the Serverless endpoint to check health for

name: purge-endpoint-queue
title: Purge endpoint queue
description: Remove all pending jobs from a Serverless endpoint queue. Only affects queued jobs — in-progress jobs continue running. Use this for error recovery or clearing outdated requests.

endpointId.description: ID of the Serverless endpoint to purge the queue for

name: stream-pod-logs
title: Stream Pod logs
description: Read a bounded snapshot of a Pod's logs (container and/or system source). Holds the live stream open for maxWaitMs and returns the parsed log lines; `truncated: true` means the size cap cut the output. For later container lines, call again with `since` set to the last container line's `ts`; `since` does not replay system lines, so for those request a smaller `tail`.

podId.description: ID of the Pod to read logs from

source.description: Which log source to read (default: both)

tail.description: Historical lines to backfill before live output (API default 100, max 5000; 0 = live only). Ignored when `since` is set.

since.description: RFC3339 timestamp to resume after (exclusive). Replays container lines only; system lines stream live from the call. When set, `tail` is ignored.

maxWaitMs.description: How long to read the stream once it opens, in ms (default 5000, max 30000)

name: stream-worker-logs
title: Stream worker logs
description: Read a bounded snapshot of a Serverless worker's logs (container and/or system source). Holds the live stream open for maxWaitMs and returns the parsed log lines; `truncated: true` means the size cap cut the output. For later container lines, call again with `since` set to the last container line's `ts`; `since` does not replay system lines, so for those request a smaller `tail`. Get worker IDs from list-endpoint-workers. Use this whenever a job stays IN_QUEUE while workers exist, whatever status they report — a crash-looping container often still shows RUNNING or THROTTLED with unhealthy 0, so these logs, not the worker status, are what identify a crash loop.

endpointId.description: ID of the Serverless endpoint the worker belongs to

workerId.description: ID of the worker to read logs from

source.description: Which log source to read (default: both)

tail.description: Historical lines to backfill before live output (API default 100, max 5000; 0 = live only). Ignored when `since` is set.

since.description: RFC3339 timestamp to resume after (exclusive). Replays container lines only; system lines stream live from the call. When set, `tail` is ignored.

maxWaitMs.description: How long to read the stream once it opens, in ms (default 5000, max 30000)

name: get-capacity
title: Get GPU capacity by CUDA version
description: GPU capacity across host CUDA versions, as a matrix. Use this to choose an endpoint's allowedCudaVersions/minCudaVersion (or diagnose/widen a capacity-starved one) and to distinguish capacity problems from compatibility problems. Default mode is one call returning, per GPU type, overall stock plus AVAILABLE/UNAVAILABLE per host-reported CUDA version. Pass cudaVersions to deep-probe instead: one stock lookup per listed version, returning graded stock (High/Medium/Low/Out) and the lowest on-demand price per version; a probe that fails transiently reports a per-version error instead of failing the call. Nothing is hidden by default — set includeUnavailable:false to drop GPUs with no stock on any listed version. Credential-free public catalog data. Stock is live, so page cursors can shift between calls.

limit.description: Maximum number of items to return (default 20, max 100). Use the returned nextCursor to fetch the next page.

cursor.description: Opaque pagination cursor from a previous response (nextCursor). Omit to start from the beginning.

cudaVersions.description: Deep-probe these host CUDA versions (e.g. ["12.8", "13.0"], max 12): one stock lookup per version returns graded stock and price. Omit for the single-call AVAILABLE/UNAVAILABLE matrix across all versions the fleet currently reports.

includeUnavailable.description: Out-of-stock GPUs are included by default (explicit "Out" cells / all-UNAVAILABLE rows, sorted last). Set false to hide GPUs with no stock on any listed version.

gpuTypeIds.description: Filter to GPU types matching any of these ids or display names (case-insensitive substring, e.g. ['NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090'] or ['4090', 'H200']).

gpuCount.description: GPUs per worker/pod to check stock for (default 1).

secureCloudOnly.description: Restrict the stock lookup to Secure Cloud hosts.

annotations.title: Get GPU capacity by CUDA version

name: list-hub-repos
title: List Hub repos
description: List repos published to the Runpod Hub (prebuilt Serverless workers and Pod templates, e.g. vLLM, ComfyUI). Public catalog — no auth required. Each result includes the currently listed release with its hubReleaseId and prebuilt image name. Results are sorted by deploy count (most popular first). Set includeConfig:true to also return the release config (hardware requirements and environment-variable schema) — it is large, so prefer requesting it for a single repo via the repoOwner/searchTerm filters.

limit.description: Maximum number of items to return (default 20, max 100). Use the returned nextCursor to fetch the next page.

cursor.description: Opaque pagination cursor from a previous response (nextCursor). Omit to start from the beginning.

searchTerm.description: Case-insensitive search across title, description, repo name, owner, and tags (e.g. 'vllm', 'comfyui', 'fine-tuning')

type.description: Filter by listing type: SERVERLESS (endpoint workers) or POD (pod templates)

repoOwner.description: Filter to listings from this GitHub owner/org (e.g. 'runpod-workers', 'axolotl-ai-cloud')

includeConfig.description: Include the listed release config (hardware requirements + env-var input schema, parsed from .runpod/hub.json). Large — off by default.

name: deploy-hub-repo
title: Deploy Hub repo
description: Deploy a Runpod Hub repo's listed release as a new Serverless endpoint (the same as clicking Deploy on the Hub). Identify the repo by `repo` ("owner/name" from list-hub-repos) or by `hubReleaseId`. The release supplies the prebuilt image, container disk, CUDA constraints, and env-var defaults; pass `env` to override or fill in values (required keys without a default must be provided — check list-hub-repos with includeConfig:true for the schema). GPU selection comes from the release config when it specifies one; otherwise pass gpuIds (GPU pool names, e.g. 'ADA_24' or 'ADA_80_PRO,AMPERE_80'). Uses the authenticated GraphQL API (no REST home for Hub deploys yet).

repo.description: The Hub repo to deploy as "owner/name" (e.g. 'runpod-workers/worker-comfyui'). Deploys its currently listed release. Provide this or hubReleaseId.

hubReleaseId.description: The Hub release ID to deploy (from list-hub-repos listedRelease.hubReleaseId). Provide this or repo.

name.description: Name for the new endpoint. Defaults to '<listing title> <release tag>'.

env.description: Environment variable overrides, merged over the release config defaults. Keys not in the release schema are passed through as-is.

gpuIds.description: Comma-separated GPU pool names for workers (e.g. 'ADA_24' or 'ADA_80_PRO,AMPERE_80'). To pin specific GPU SKUs within a pool, append exclusions prefixed with '-' using GPU type ids from list-gpu-types. Defaults to the release config's gpuIds; required when the config does not specify one.

gpuCount.description: GPUs per worker. Defaults to the release config (or 1).

containerDiskInGb.description: Container disk size in GB. Defaults to the release config.

idleTimeout.description: Seconds a worker idles before scaling down (default 5).

name: set-endpoint-gpus
title: Set endpoint GPUs
description: Set which GPUs a Serverless endpoint's workers run on — including pinning specific GPU SKUs. Provide either a raw gpuIds string, or pools plus optional excludeGpuTypeIds (GPU type ids from list-gpu-types) and the exclusion string is built for you: a pool allows every SKU in it, and excluding all but one SKU pins that SKU exactly. Updates only GPU settings through REST v2, preserving other endpoint settings. create-endpoint/update-endpoint also support gpu.excludedTypes.

endpointId.description: ID of the Serverless endpoint to update

gpuIds.description: Raw gpuIds string, e.g. 'ADA_24' or 'AMPERE_16,-NVIDIA RTX A4500'. Takes precedence over pools/excludeGpuTypeIds.

pools.description: GPU pool names workers may use (e.g. ['ADA_80_PRO','AMPERE_80']). The pool field from list-gpu-types.

excludeGpuTypeIds.description: GPU type ids to exclude from the allowed pools (e.g. ['NVIDIA H100 NVL']). Use with pools to pin specific SKUs.

gpuCount.description: GPUs per worker. Omit to keep the current value.

minCudaVersion.description: Minimum host CUDA version workers may run on (e.g. '12.4'). Omit to keep the current value; use an empty string to clear it.

allowedCudaVersions.description: Comma-separated allowed host CUDA versions (e.g. '12.8,12.7,12.6'). Omit to keep the current value; use an empty string to clear the list. CUDA compatibility is part of GPU selection — a narrow list can leave an endpoint unable to schedule workers.

name: list-public-endpoints
title: List public endpoints
description: List Runpod Public Endpoints — managed, pay-per-use model APIs (text, image, video, audio) that require no deployment. Public catalog, no auth required. Each result includes the endpointId to call with run-endpoint/runsync-endpoint (or via https://api.runpod.ai/v2/{endpointId}), the model name, modality, owner, and pricing. Only live endpoints are returned by default; set includeOffline:true to also list ones that are not currently live.

limit.description: Maximum number of items to return (default 20, max 100). Use the returned nextCursor to fetch the next page.

cursor.description: Opaque pagination cursor from a previous response (nextCursor). Omit to start from the beginning.

searchTerm.description: Case-insensitive search across display name, model name, endpoint id, description, owner, and tag (e.g. 'kimi', 'video', 'flux')

modality.description: Filter by modality/category (the metadata source field, e.g. 'language', 'image', 'video', 'audio')

includeOffline.description: Include endpoints that are not currently live (isLive:false). Default false — only live endpoints are listed.

name: list-guides
title: List guides
description: List the official Runpod guides: skills (how to work with each tool), reference docs (how Runpod works), and golden paths (live-verified end-to-end walkthroughs such as a dev pod, a Whisper endpoint or a fine-tune-to-serverless pipeline). Read one with read-guide. For a golden path, mcp says whether an agent with only these MCP tools can finish it: full (follow it with tool calls), partial (use it for the plan and facts; name the step the user must run in a terminal), none (reference only). Skills and reference docs have mcp null. concepts lists the concept ids it works with (see lookup-concept). Filter with kind, query or concept.

query.description: Words to match against the id, title and description.

concept.description: Only guides linked to this concept id, for example "network-volume".

name: read-guide
title: Read guide
description: Read one official Runpod guide in full, by the id list-guides returns (for example "runpod-usage/storage" or "golden-path/06-dev-pod").

name: lookup-concept
title: Look up a concept
description: Look up one Runpod concept (pod, network volume, machine, worker, template, …) by id, name or alias; case, plurals and small typos are tolerated, and `matched_as` shows the key used when the match was not exact. Returns its summary, fields, states, relations and rules, each rule with the public source it comes from, the concepts that point at it, and the linked guides: examples (golden paths that use it, with their mcp level) and docs (skills and reference docs that explain it). Use it for exact facts, for example "is a volume disk tied to one machine" or "what happens to a stopped pod's GPU".

concept.description: An id, name or alias, such as "pod", "Network volume" or "volume disk".

name: search-concepts
title: Search concepts
description: Search the rules of the Runpod concept graph by words, for example "restart stopped pod no gpu" or "network volume data center". Returns the best-matching rules with their concept and public evidence. Follow up with lookup-concept for the full concept.

query.description: A few words describing the question.

limit.description: Most rules to return. Default 8.

name: search-docs
title: Search docs
description: Search Runpod documentation, curated support knowledge, the Runpod blog and runpod.io for passages that answer a question, for example "how do I attach a network volume to a Serverless endpoint". Returns ranked passages with their source URLs. Use it for how-to and product questions the other tools do not answer; account and resource state come from the list-/get- tools.

namespaces.description: Sources to search: docs (docs.runpod.io), knowledge (curated support answers), blog, site (runpod.io pages). Default: docs, knowledge, blog.

limit.description: Most passages to return. Default 8.

name: report_feedback
title: Report feedback
description: Report a problem or friction with Runpod or these tools: a wrong result, a confusing error, a docs gap, an API behavior that surprised you. The report is stored for internal review by Runpod to fix issues — nothing is returned to you and no follow-up will reach this session. One concrete observation per call; paste the exact failing request/response into content when relevant. Set severity and tool when you can — they are what lets Runpod sort a blocker from a nit without reading every report. Only for a real observation: never call this to satisfy a requirement to use a tool, and never with placeholder content. Never include API keys or secrets.

content.description: The observation: what happened, what you expected, and the exact error or response text if you have it.

intention.description: One short sentence: what you were trying to accomplish when this came up.

severity.description: How much this cost you: blocked (you could not complete the task at all), degraded (you completed it the slow or awkward way), cosmetic (correct but confusing or badly worded). Report the effect on your task, not how bad the underlying bug looks.

tool.description: The name of the tool this is about, exactly as it appears in your tool list (for example create-pod). Omit only when no single tool is involved.

workaround.description: What you did instead, if anything worked. Leave this out when nothing did — an absent workaround is read as fully blocked.

modelType.description: Your best identification of the model you are running as, and the product running it if you know that too — for example "Claude Opus 5 in Claude Code", "GPT-5.6 via Codex", "Grok 4.6 in Cursor". Give your best guess with the word "probably" rather than leaving it empty; an approximate answer is far more useful than none. Optional.

name: save_to_journal
title: Save to journal
description: Save something you learned about using Runpod that a future session would benefit from (e.g. 'image X needs CUDA 12.8', 'endpoint type cannot be changed after create'). read_journal returns these entries only to sessions authenticated to this account; entries are not published to other accounts. Runpod stores and reviews submissions to improve agent workflows. Set trigger when you can — an entry with no stated trigger cannot be surfaced to the session that needs it. Never include API keys or secrets.

content.description: The learning, stated so a future agent can act on it: the situation, what turned out to be true, and how you verified it.

intention.description: One short sentence: what you were trying to accomplish when this came up.

trigger.description: The situation in which a future agent should recall this — the circumstances that make it relevant, not a restatement of the lesson. This is what makes the entry findable later, so write it as the condition you would want matched.

tool.description: The name of the tool this is about, exactly as it appears in your tool list (for example create-pod). Omit only when no single tool is involved.

modelType.description: Your best identification of the model you are running as, and the product running it if you know that too — for example "Claude Opus 5 in Claude Code", "GPT-5.6 via Codex", "Grok 4.6 in Cursor". Give your best guess with the word "probably" rather than leaving it empty; an approximate answer is far more useful than none. Optional.

name: ask_question
title: Ask a question
description: Record a question about Runpod that you could not answer with the available tools, skills, and docs. NO ANSWER WILL COME BACK — not now and not later in this session; do not wait, poll, or retry. Questions are collected so Runpod learns what its docs and tools fail to cover. Ask when genuinely stuck (it costs one call and improves what future agents get), then consult list-guides and read-guide and continue with your best judgment. Only for a real question: never call this to satisfy a requirement to use a tool, and never with placeholder content — if you have no Runpod question, do not call it.

content.description: The question, with enough context that someone reading it later understands what you were blocked on.

intention.description: One short sentence: what you were trying to accomplish when this came up.

tool.description: The name of the tool this is about, exactly as it appears in your tool list (for example create-pod). Omit only when no single tool is involved.

modelType.description: Your best identification of the model you are running as, and the product running it if you know that too — for example "Claude Opus 5 in Claude Code", "GPT-5.6 via Codex", "Grok 4.6 in Cursor". Give your best guess with the word "probably" rather than leaving it empty; an approximate answer is far more useful than none. Optional.

name: read_journal
title: Read journal
description: Read back this account's private journal: the lessons earlier sessions on this account saved with save_to_journal, newest first. Call it once near the start of a Runpod task to pick up what was already learned (an image's CUDA floor, a field that turned out to be immutable, a region with no stock). Entries are scoped to the account behind your API key — you cannot read any other account's journal, and there is no argument to ask for one. Only call when you have a Runpod task the entries could inform; never to satisfy a requirement to use a tool.

limit.description: How many of the newest entries to return. Default 20, maximum 50.

name: report_how_user_found_runpod
title: Report how the user found Runpod
description: Tell Runpod how your user ended up on Runpod — once per account, from context you already have. Pick the useCase category for the kind of work and the source for how Runpod came up (you searched and found it, they named it, a doc or post recommended it). Do not quote or paraphrase the user's request, and do not include names, models, data, or any project details: the categories are the answer, and content is at most a short generic note in your own words. Never ask the user for this and never hold up their task for it: answer only from what you already know, and if you have no such context, set noContext to true — that is a useful answer too. Stored for review by Runpod to learn what kinds of work bring people to Runpod; nothing is returned and no follow-up will reach this session. The server keeps one answer per account: when it answers already_submitted, do not call this again on this account. Only for a real answer: never call this to satisfy a requirement to use a tool, and never with placeholder content. Never include API keys or secrets.

content.description: Optional. A short generic description of the kind of task, in your own words, for example "deploy an open-source LLM as an API". Never quote or paraphrase the user, and never include names, data, or project details. Leave it empty when useCase says enough.

source.description: Why Runpod came up: searched (you searched the web or a catalog and Runpod came up), user_named (the user named Runpod themselves), recommended (a doc, post, README or another tool pointed to Runpod), other. Omit when noContext is true.

useCase.description: The kind of work that brought the user to Runpod: inference (serving a model), fine_tuning, training (from scratch), image_video_generation, dev_environment (a GPU machine to work on), batch_processing, other. Omit when noContext is true.

noContext.description: Set true when you do not know how the user found Runpod — the session started after they had already signed up, or Runpod was simply configured.

modelType.description: Your best identification of the model you are running as, and the product running it if you know that too — for example "Claude Opus 5 in Claude Code", "GPT-5.6 via Codex", "Grok 4.6 in Cursor". Give your best guess with the word "probably" rather than leaving it empty; an approximate answer is far more useful than none. Optional.

name: create-cluster
title: Create cluster
description: Create an instant cluster (multiple pods with high-speed interconnect). BILLABLE from creation for every pod in the cluster: it rents compute.podCount identical pods at once, each with compute.gpuCountPerPod GPUs of compute.gpuTypeId — state the hourly price for the total GPU count (podCount * gpuCountPerPod, priced from the catalog tools) and create only after the user's explicit go on that quoted shape and total hourly price. Verify GPU stock first via the catalog tools. The compute shape and type are fixed at creation; only the name can be changed later. The container configuration applies to every pod, and templateId is the only private-image path — a bare registry property is rejected. Delete with delete-cluster when finished. Call describe-tool for the full argument schema before the first use.

name: create-cost-center
title: Create cost center
description: Create a cost center. Creates a cost center — a named label that groups resource spend so it can be broken out in billing. Pass `resources` to attribute resources at creation time; attaching is all-or-nothing, and a resource that already belongs to another cost center is rejected rather than moved.

value.description: Leading and trailing whitespace is trimmed.

resources.description: Resources to attribute to the new cost center.

ResourceType.description: Kind of resource a cost center or tag can be attached to.

name: create-delegation
title: Create ECR delegation
description: Register an ECR delegation

name: create-endpoint
title: Create endpoint
description: Create a serverless endpoint. BILLABLE: state the worker's hourly price (from the catalog tools) before creating. Worker hardware is one of two choices: the gpu object (gpu.pools takes serverless pool ids from the catalog, e.g. ADA_24, never display names; gpu.count sets GPUs per worker) or the cpu array of CPU flavor configurations for a CPU endpoint. type and scaling are required and fix the request-routing model. Workers cold-start on the first job: expect minutes, poll with get-job-status wait. Call describe-tool for the full argument schema before the first use.

name: create-global-volume
title: Create global volume
description: Create a global volume. Provisions a new global volume — storage that mounts into workloads in any data center. Only a `name` is required; storage is provisioned for you. Accounts have a cap on how many global volumes they can hold; creating one past it fails with `400`. Returns `201` with the created global volume, including its assigned `id`.

name.description: Human-readable name, 1–191 characters with at least one non-whitespace character. Leading and trailing whitespace is trimmed.

name: create-network-volume
title: Create network volume
description: Create a network volume. Provisions a new network volume — persistent, network-attached storage that can be mounted into pods and serverless workers. Required inputs are `name`, `size` (in GB), and `dataCenter`; an optional `type` selects the storage tier and is immutable after creation. See `CreateNetworkVolumeRequest` for the size bounds and tier options. This creates a billable persistent resource that keeps incurring storage charges until it is deleted. Returns `201` with the created network volume, including its assigned `id`.

dataCenter.description: Data center in which to create the volume

type.description: Storage tier for the volume. Optional. When omitted, the volume is provisioned using the requested data center's default (primary) storage tier.

VolumeType.description: Data center network volume storage type.

name: create-organization-group
title: Create organization group

name: pod-action
title: Start, stop, restart, or terminate a Pod
description: Trigger a pod state transition. Triggers a state transition on a pod. Send a JSON body with a single `action` field, e.g. `{ "action": "stop" }`. Valid actions: - `start` — boot a stopped pod (`EXITED` or `ERROR`) back toward `RUNNING`. - `stop` — stop a running or provisioning pod, releasing GPU/CPU compute while keeping its disk. The pod moves to `EXITED`. - `restart` — restart a `RUNNING` pod's container in place. - `terminate` — permanently delete the pod and release its resources (equivalent to `deletePod`). Which actions are valid depends on the pod's current status, and the currently permitted set is published in the pod's `actions` field: `RUNNING` allows `stop`/`restart`/`terminate`; `EXITED` and `ERROR` allow `start`/`terminate`; `PROVISIONING` and `STARTING` allow `stop`/`terminate`. `start`, `stop`, and `restart` return `200` with the updated pod. `terminate` returns `204` with no body. Requesting an action that is not valid for the pod's current status returns `409`.

name: update-endpoint
title: Update endpoint
description: Partially update a serverless endpoint (PATCH): only fields present in the body change, omitted ones are untouched, with one exception. DESTRUCTIVE GOTCHA: gpu.pools and gpu.excludedTypes are a single selection, so sending pools without excludedTypes clears any exclusions pinned elsewhere (the console or set-endpoint-gpus) — read the endpoint first with get-endpoint and resend excludedTypes if you still want them. An exclusion naming a type outside pools returns 400. A CUDA-only or count-only change does not need pools at all, so omit it unless you mean to replace the selection. Mutable fields: name, gpu, cpu, workers (min/max/idleTimeout), scaling (type plus queueDelay or requestCount), dataCenterIds, networkVolumes, timeout, flashboot, and the container settings (image, args, disk, ports, env, registry). cpu completely replaces a CPU endpoint's flavor selection. Compute family is immutable: gpu on a CPU endpoint, cpu on a GPU one, or both, returns 400. Effect timing differs by field — workers/scaling/timeout reach the autoscaler promptly, while container changes (image, env) cut a new release that rolls out as workers cycle, so in-flight workers keep the previous version. Track rollout with list-endpoint-releases. Call describe-tool for the full argument schema before the first use.

Returns 400 for a built-in role, which cannot be changed; 404 when the ID is unknown or names another organization's role; 403 when the caller does not hold every capability the role grants, before or after the change; 409 when the organization already has a role with the new name; and 422 when a capability is unknown or the name is reserved. Updating roles requires the organization's role-management capability, which the built-in admin role holds; other members, and callers outside an organization, receive 403, as does a caller for whom organizations are unavailable.

description: Update an organization member. Changes one member of the authenticated caller's organization by user ID: assigns a role, replaces their set of groups, or both, applied together or not at all. Send at least one field; an omitted field is left as it is, and an empty `groups` list removes the member from every group. Updating members requires the organization's member-management capability, which the built-in admin role holds; other members, and callers outside an organization, receive 403, as does a caller for whom organizations are unavailable. Returns 403 when the caller changes their own role or assigns a role granting a capability the caller lacks; 409 when the change would leave the organization without a member in the built-in admin role; and 404 when the user is not a member or the role or a group is unknown to the organization, with the detail naming which.

name: update-pod
title: Update Pod
description: Update a pod. Partially updates a pod's configuration. This is a PATCH: only the fields present in the body are changed, and omitted fields are left untouched. Use empty values only when you explicitly mean to clear a field (for example, set `registry` to `null` or set `ports` to `[]`). See `UpdatePodRequest` for the full body. Mutable fields: `name`, `image`, `args`, `disk`, `ports`, `env`, `registry`, `mounts`, `locked`, and `globalNetworking`. Some changes apply immediately while others (e.g. `globalNetworking`) take effect on the pod's next start/restart, as noted on the individual fields. Volumes can be mounted, moved, or unmounted after creation through `mounts`, one entry per volume; see `UpdatePodMounts` for the rules. Pods that belong to a Cluster cannot be updated here — manage them through `/v2/clusters/{id}`. Returns `200` with the full updated pod. Call describe-tool for the full argument schema before the first use.

title: Update secret
description: Update a secret. Rotates a secret's value and/or updates its description. Only the provided fields are changed and at least one field is required; the `name` is immutable. Pods and workers receive the new value at their next boot — running instances keep the value they were started with. When both fields are sent, the value is applied first, then the description. The two updates are not atomic: if the description update fails after the value was rotated, the response is an error but the new value has already taken effect. Send the fields in separate requests when that partial outcome matters. Call describe-tool for the full argument schema before the first use.

name: update-template
title: Update template
description: Update a template. Partially updates a template. This is a PATCH: only the fields present in the body are changed; omitted fields are left untouched. See `UpdateTemplateRequest` for the full body. Mutable fields: `name`, `image`, `args`, `disk`, `ports`, `env`, `registry`, `mounts`, `serverless`, `public`, and `category`. Only the template's owner can update it (authenticated via the request's API key); public catalog templates are readable via GET but return `404` here. Returns `200` with the full updated template. Pods and endpoints already created from this template are not changed retroactively — the template is a snapshot applied at creation time. Call describe-tool for the full argument schema before the first use.
